newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian union launches bans on Indonesian ships.
newsitem.headline: Australian union launches bans on Indonesian ships.

text.p: Australia's powerful Maritime Union announced on Wednesday it would impose rolling bans on Indonesian shipping in protest against the recent arrest of two Indonesian independent labour leaders.

"The bans are to protest against the recent arrests of independent labour leaders Muchtar Pakpahan and Dita Sari and the continuing repression following the July riots in Jakarta," the union said in a statement.
The first ship to be hit by the rolling bans will be the Bogasari Empat, due to arrive in Fremantle on the Western Australia coast late on Wednesday to load wheat, it said.
The ship will load wheat as scheduled but will not be allowed to leave right away after loading. Instead it will be delayed 24 hours,
"We in effect will apply the ban when it finishes loading so there will be a 24-hour delay (to the ship's departure)," union assistant secretary Vic Slater told Reuters.
The rolling bans are also a response to Australian Prime Minister John Howard's failure in Jakarta this week to press Indonesia on the issue of human rights and democracy, the union said.

Pakpahan, leader of the Indonesian Labour Welfare Union (SBSI), has been charged with subversion in connection with riots that rocked the Indonesian capital on July 27. The crime of subversion is punishable by death.

Five people died and 149 were injured in the riots, Indonesia's official Human Rights Commission has said. Scores of buildings were set ablaze in the unrest, which was the worst in Jakarta since anti-Japanese riots there in 1974.

The Australian rolling bans are in line with a world-wide campaign against Pakpahan's arrest by the International Transport Workers' Federation, which represents over five million workers in 120 countries, the Maritime Union said.
"Muchtar Pakpahan is an independent and moderate union leader who has even won the respect of the U.S. embassy (in Jakarta)," Slater said.
Bans on Indonesian shipping will be announced as they are applied to specific ships, and the campaign will be reviewed at an undisclosed future date, he said.
"It is certainly something we are committed to, but we will review things in the context of all sorts of things," he added.
The Maritime Union has 10,000 members around Australia, working as seamen and waterside workers, Slater said.
